question: What does an AI systems performance engineer do, and why does hardware-software codesign (mechanical sympathy) and goodput matter at ultrascale?
hypothesis: At ultrascale, clever software and algorithm codesign beats brute-force hardware spending.
contributions: Frames the AI systems performance engineer role and responsibilities
Uses DeepSeek-V3/R1 on H800s as a codesign case
Defines goodput as useful throughput normalised by peak
Gives a book roadmap by chapter

results.claim: Goodput worked example: 8 GPUs process 100,000 tokens in 10 s against a 12,000 tok/s peak gives 83.3% efficiency.
results.setup: Illustrative node of 8 GPUs, 1,500 tokens/s peak per GPU; goodput = useful tokens or requests per unit time, normalised by peak.

results.claim: Training job at 300 of 1,000 samples/s ideal is 30% goodput.
results.setup: Hypothetical job with poor input pipeline and excess synchronisation.
results.quote: it achieves only 300 samples/second of actual training through-

results.claim: Meta's Revisiting Reliability analysis: a cluster appearing 100% utilised lost 70-75% of compute to overheads (communication delays, suboptimal parallelisation, data delays, failure recovery).
results.setup: Meta training clusters; chapter gives no model, cluster size or date beyond a 2025 paper.
results.note: Chapter says the lost share came from communication delays, suboptimal parallelization, data delays or failure recovery, not only failures.

results.claim: MLPerf Training v5.0: GB200 NVL72 gives up to 2.6x per-GPU training throughput over equivalent Hopper.
results.setup: MLPerf Training v5.0 (2025), GB200 NVL72 vs Hopper; MLPerf cautions per-GPU is not a primary cross-platform metric.

results.claim: MLPerf Inference v5.0: Blackwell NVL72 about 3.4x per-GPU inference throughput over equivalent Hopper cluster.
results.setup: MLPerf Inference v5.0 (2025); attributed to higher per-GPU performance and larger NVLink domain.

results.claim: H800 NVLink is about 400 GB/s per GPU versus about 900 GB/s on H100.
results.setup: H800 vs H100 (900 GB/s); H100 memory bandwidth 3.35 TB/s.
results.quote: while H800 provides about 400 GB/s bandwidth per GPU
results.note: Chapter says HBM capacity and bandwidth are 'largely similar' yet later says the H800's 'limited throughput means that data transfers are much slower'.

results.claim: DeepSeek-V3 is a ~680B-parameter MoE with about 37B active per token, 1 shared plus 8 of 256 routed experts (9 active).
results.setup: DeepSeek-V3/R1, per DeepSeek technical report as relayed by the book.
results.quote: uses only about 37 billion active parameters per input token
results.note: Chapter prints ~680 billion total; published figure is 671B (not stated in chapter).

results.claim: DeepSeek claims DeepSeek-R1 trained for under $6 million in compute; the book doubts what it covers.
results.setup: DeepSeek claim; GPT-4 est. ~$100M, Gemini Ultra est. ~$191M. Unclear if it covers one run only.
results.quote: DeepSeek claims that their DeepSeek-R1 model was trained for less than $6 mil-

results.claim: NVIDIA stock fell about 17% in one day after the DeepSeek announcement.
results.setup: NVIDIA share price after DeepSeek-R1 news, late 2024/early 2025.

results.claim: 100T-parameter model in 16-bit needs about 182 TB of GPU memory just for weights, nearly 1,000 B200 GPUs (180 GB usable) or 700 B300.
results.setup: Weights only, 2 bytes per parameter; excludes activations, optimiser state and inference input; ~125 B200 nodes of 8.
results.note: The printed formula '182 TB = 100 trillion parameters x 16 bits per weight x 8 bits per byte' is garbled; 100T x 2 bytes = 200 TB.

results.claim: A dense 100T-parameter model on about 29T tokens needs on the order of 1.2 x 10^? FLOPS; the exponent did not survive extraction.
results.setup: Dense model, 29 trillion tokens; exponent lost in text extraction.

results.claim: GB200 NVL72 rack: about 1.44 exaFLOPS FP4 (2:1 sparsity), about 720 petaFLOPS FP8 (2:1 sparsity).
results.setup: FP4 with 2 to 1 structured sparsity; theoretical peak.

results.claim: GB200 NVL72 has about 13.5 TB HBM3e (192 GB x 72) and about 30 TB including Grace CPU memory.
results.setup: 72 Blackwell GPUs at 192 GB; rack is not one uniform memory device.

results.claim: GB200 NVL72 rack power is about 120 to 132 kW depending on vendor and cooling.
NVLink 5 gives 1.8 TB/s bidirectional per GPU, about 130 TB/s aggregate within one NVL72 domain.
FlashAttention gives a 2x-4x speedup in training and inference for long sequences versus default attention.
results.setup: Long sequences; no model or hardware stated.

results.claim: Google's Switch Transformer (1.6T MoE, 2021) trained 7x faster than a comparable dense approach at the same accuracy.
results.quote: It was trained 7× faster than a comparable dense approach.

results.claim: A 20% boost in cluster efficiency can save millions of dollars of hardware at large scale.
results.quote: Consider a performance engineer helping to achieve a 20% boost in cluster efficiency.

limits: Many numbers are quoted without citation (FlashAttention 2-4x, Switch 7x, GPT-4 and Gemini costs, Meta 70-75%).
Chapter text conflicts on H800 memory (largely similar vs much slower) and prints ~680B for DeepSeek-V3 total parameters.
The 182 TB formula is garbled; the 100T FLOPs exponent is lost in extraction.
Training-cluster focus: goodput is defined for training clusters and by useful work per peak, not by an SLO.
Hardware roadmap (Rubin 2026, Feynman 2028) is a forecast; $6M DeepSeek claim is disputed by the author.
practices: Measure goodput, not raw FLOPS or utilisation, using Nsight Systems/Compute or the PyTorch profiler (Key Takeaways).
Set up automated performance tests to catch regressions early (Benchmarking and Profiling).
Use a profile-driven loop: hypothesis, reproducible benchmark, adjust, rerun, share (Transparency and Reproducibility).
Compare hardware by system-level end-to-end throughput, not per-GPU MLPerf numbers (MLPerf aside).
On Grace Blackwell managed memory, prefer explicit cudaMemPrefetchAsync and cudaMemAdvise to reduce page-fault stalls (NVL72 section).
Overlap communication with computation and prefetch/cache data to raise goodput (Goodput section).
Treat communication bandwidth as scarce and codesign hardware, software and algorithms (DeepSeek section).
